passage: I'm Himani. My goal was a set of proper art pens, and I had a chart, a tin and a date. Then March happened: a school project that needed materials, a class trip fee, and a broken geometry set. The tin lost most of a month. I sat on my bed staring at the chart, and the thought crept in: what's the point? My cousin Trisha said, “You don't have to quit, just move the finish line.” So I pushed the target date four weeks later and put a little less into the tin each week, so it wouldn't squeeze me on top of everything else. It felt like a small defeat at first. But the tin started filling again, slowly, and I liked that I hadn't torn up the chart.

qa.a: Himani pushed the target date four weeks later.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling when staring at the chart?
qa.a: Himani felt discouraged, since the thought crept in: what's the point?

qa.a: Himani could earn a little through small honest work or trim one spending area, since the plan stays while income or costs shift.

qa.q: How might Trisha see Himani's changed plan?
qa.a: Trisha probably feels relieved and glad, since the advice to move the finish line helped Himani keep going.

Maths teacher's note, savings project check-in, October
Zeenat's target was a secondhand tablet for her drawing, with a goal date of 15 December and a fixed weekly amount. Through August and September she hit every week.
Then October happened: a school trip fee, a new geometry box after hers was lost, and a costume for annual day. She had to use some of the saved money, and three weeks' saving went into these instead.
At the check-in she looked frustrated. Her classmate Joseph, whose plan had also slipped, said he was going to give up. Zeenat didn't. She redid the numbers in front of me: move the date four weeks later, to 12 January, and save a slightly smaller amount each week, which she said felt “doable, not punishing”.
She crossed out the old date on her chart and wrote the new one. Joseph asked her to help him redo his.

qa.q: What was Zeenat's new goal date?
What was Zeenat feeling at the check-in?
qa.a: Zeenat looked frustrated about the October costs, but determined not to give up.

qa.q: What might Zeenat do if another unexpected cost comes up?
qa.a: Adjust the plan again, perhaps with a parent's input, rather than abandoning it, since a later date still reaches the goal.

qa.q: How might Joseph see Zeenat's new plan?
qa.a: Joseph, who planned to quit, sees another option and feels encouraged enough to ask for help redoing his own.

grounding: A teacher notes a student who, after unexpected school costs, moves her target date four weeks later and lowers the weekly amount instead of abandoning the plan.

passage:
Wednesday
Bad month for the savings plan. The goal was a pair of football boots by 30 November, saving the same amount every week. Then school asked for a lab manual, a new tie (mine tore), and money for the Children's Day class party. My jar went down instead of up.
My first thought was to give up. I told Farhan, and he said, “Just forget the boots, man.”
But tonight I sat down and looked at it properly. The boots aren't gone. The date is just wrong now. If I move it four weeks, to 28 December, I can save a bit less each week and still get there. A smaller number I'll actually manage beats a bigger one I'll quit.
I rewrote the plan on a fresh page and showed Ammi. She said it looked sensible.
New date: 28 December.
– Vijay

qa.q: What is the new date for the boots?
How did Vijay feel after the bad month?
qa.a: Vijay felt discouraged enough to consider giving up, then calmer once the plan was rewritten.

qa.q: What else could Vijay do to protect the new plan?
qa.a: Keep a short note of school costs that might come up, and check the plan with Ammi each month.

qa.q: How might Farhan see Vijay's new page?
qa.a: Farhan, who said to forget the boots, may be surprised that a changed date keeps the goal alive.

grounding: Shows a student who, after a month of unexpected school costs, moves the target date four weeks later and lowers the weekly amount instead of quitting.
